name: Produce
tagline: A small indie productivity SaaS whose public surface says less about what it does than most people would like.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: This one gets graded on its class rather than its feature list, because the feature list is not something we can verify yet. Products in this bucket, single-purpose indie productivity tools built by a tiny team, are almost always a thin layer of opinionated UI over a database you could define in twenty minutes. An agent will get you a local, keyboard-driven version of the core loop in a session, and it will feel surprisingly fine. What it will not get you is the part that makes people pay: the taste in the defaults, the mobile client, and sync that works when your laptop is shut. Treat this as a weekend build with real edges, not a drop-in replacement.
coreLoopDIY: Spins up a local-first, keyboard-driven workspace where you capture items, group them into projects, and plan a day, all stored in a single SQLite file you own.
requirements: A machine you are willing to leave running if you want it reachable from elsewhere
Optional: Tailscale or similar if you want access from your phone
whatYouLose: A real mobile app, which is where most productivity tools actually get used
Sync across devices without you volunteering as the sysadmin
The small interaction details that someone spent months sanding down
Any integrations with calendars, email, or trackers unless you wire each one yourself
Someone else deciding what the product should not do, which is most of the value in this category
moatNotes: The moat in small productivity apps is almost never technical. It is one person's refusal to add the feature you asked for.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the gap between a working tool and a tool you keep using every morning is mostly polish, and polish is the single thing a one-shot build cannot fake. People pay small monthly amounts to not think about their task system: it is on their phone, it syncs, it has sensible defaults, and nothing breaks after an OS update. A self-hosted clone shifts that maintenance onto you, and the usual outcome is that you abandon it in three weeks and go back to paying.
notes: Graded on the category, not on verified features, so take the confidence rating seriously.
prompt:
Build a local-first personal productivity workspace. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry, no analytics.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js 15 with the App Router and TypeScript
- Tailwind CSS, no component library
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, one file at ./data/produce.db, created on first run
- Server Actions for all mutations, no separate API layer

Data model:
- project: id, name, color, archived_at
- item: id, project_id (nullable), title, notes (markdown text), status (inbox | active | done | dropped), due_date (nullable), planned_for (date, nullable), sort_order, created_at, completed_at
- note: id, item_id (nullable), body, created_at

Views, in this order of importance:
1. Today: items where planned_for is today, plus anything overdue, grouped by project. Inline check off.
2. Inbox: unsorted capture list, with a single text field at the top that creates an item on Enter and keeps focus.
3. Projects: list of projects, click through to that project's items with drag-free reordering via keyboard only.
4. Done: last 30 days, read only.

Interaction rules:
- Keyboard first. Global hotkeys: c to capture, 1/2/3/4 to switch views, j/k to move selection, x to toggle done, t to plan for today, e to edit inline, / to search titles and notes.
- Everything must work without a mouse. Mouse support is a fallback, not the design.
- No modals except the capture field and the editor.
- Full-text search over item titles and notes using SQLite FTS5.

In scope: local HTTP server on port 3000, a JSON export endpoint, a one-command import that reads that same JSON back, and a plain npm script that backs up the db file with a timestamp.

Out of scope, do not build: auth, multi-user, email, calendar sync, recurring tasks, mobile app, notifications, any third-party integration, any paid API.

Secrets: none needed. If you add anything optional that requires a key, read it from .env and ship .env.example, and make the app run fine without it.

Deliver a README with exactly the commands to install, run, back up, and export. Seed the db with three example projects and a handful of items so the first launch is not an empty screen.
